newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda says unlikely to keep export quota.
newsitem.headline: Uganda says unlikely to keep export quota.

text.p: Ugandan coffee authorities said they were unlikely to retain any 1996/97 exports in line with an agreement by global producers in Brazil last month because drought and disease meant exports would be reduced anyway.

Officials of the state Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA) told Reuters that Uganda also did not know its exact retention position for the year because the Inter-Africa Coffee Organisation had not yet met to work out figures distribution.

"But even if such quotas are allocated, they are likely to be superceded by current (declining) procurement," a senior official at the UCDA told Reuters in Kampala. "Uganda will not need to reduce exports to meet quotas."
Industry officials have said capricious weather and disease will combine to cut Uganda's coffee exports in 1996/97 from a bumper level achieved in the previous season.
Ugandan coffee exports in 1995/96 were around 4.1 million 60-kg bags compared to 2.8 million bags in 1994/95.

Ugandan authorities have already forecast exports in the range of 3.6 million to 3.8 million bags in 1996/97 but drought and a faster-than-expected spread of the disease means the figure will be much lower than that, according to industry officials.

Uganda exported 1,290,986 bags of coffee worth $95.2 million in the first quarter of 1996/97 (October-December) from 795,502 bags worth 88.1 million in the same period last year and said the volume was the highest per quarter realised in four years.
UCDA officials forecast exports at 1,122,484 bags in the second quarter (January to March 1997) worth $90.37 million.
Traditionally, the bulk of Ugandan coffee is harvested in the first half of the coffee season (October to March), which coincides with peak consumption in the Northern hemisphere.
UCDA officials said the real impact of the poor weather and disease would be seen in a poor third quarter, and the fourth quarter would confirm the declining exports forecast.
"Given the tight supply situation, the roasters' reduced forward cover and the low stock levels with consumers, there is a likelihood of prices going upwards," a UCDA official said.
That was in reference to a sharp decline in the average unit price realised in the first quarter -- at $1.23 per kg compared to $1.84 in the same period in 1995/96.
Coffee is Uganda's dominant foreign exchange earner.
Tracheomycosis or coffee wilt disease, has affected coffees from 11 western districts and alarmed growers.
Tracheomycosis destroys a coffee tree's vascular system. It leaves a black sear on the tree stem after which the tree dies.
